Let's talk about something most folks never really mention, but it quietly shapes almost everything around us.
Why Wealth Grows Faster Than the Economy.
Imagine this: you’ve got two neighbors. The first one? Works hard day in and day out, earning a steady paycheck. The second inherited a modest chunk of money and parked it in investments. Year after year, those investments keep growing—often outpacing any raise the first neighbor might get.
Even though the first neighbor saves diligently, it’s tough to keep up. Meanwhile, the second watches their wealth multiply, almost effortlessly. Over decades, the gap between these neighbors just keeps getting wider—not because one worked harder, but simply because of how capital behaves.
Here’s the thing: this isn’t something new or rare. For centuries, the money people make from owning things—like land, stocks, or businesses—has nearly always grown faster than the overall economy. Economists have a simple way to put it: “r is greater than g.” In other words, the rate of return on capital—what you earn from investments—is usually higher than the rate at which the economy itself grows.
When that happens, people who already have wealth see it snowball, outpacing everyone else. The result? Rising inequality.
There have been rare moments when this pattern flipped—after the world wars, for example. Back then, high taxes, inflation, and the loss of old fortunes helped narrow the gap. For a while, wages actually grew faster than wealth, and more people could get ahead. But that was the exception, not the rule.
Once things settled down, the old pattern came right back. Investments started growing faster than the economy again, and the wealth gap widened.
Most of us don’t really notice this in our day-to-day lives. It shows up in things like the slow rise of house prices, the steady climb of stock markets, and how inheritance becomes more and more important. If you don’t own assets, it can feel like you’re sprinting on a treadmill—working hard, but never really catching up. If you do own assets, your wealth seems to just grow on its own.
It’s not just about luck. Our economy is set up to reward people who own things. As technology moves forward and the world gets more connected, new ways to invest keep popping up. But the basic rule hasn’t changed: if you own capital, it usually grows faster than the economy itself.
Unless something comes along to shake things up, that gap—the difference between those who own and those who don’t—will probably keep getting bigger.
And this isn’t just a money issue. When wealth outpaces economic growth, it shapes who holds power, who gets a say in big decisions, and who feels secure about the future. It touches everything, from politics to family life.
So, the quiet rule that “r is greater than g” isn’t just a technical detail. It’s a powerful force, quietly shaping the world in ways most people never even notice.
